evidence.summary: Judges 17:10 in the KJV offers the Levite ten shekels of silver “by the year”. The old Greek translation gives ten of silver for a day. The Hebrew text uses a phrase involving days.
evidence.text: KJV Judges 17:10: “And Micah said unto him, Dwell with me, and be unto me a father and a priest, and I will give thee ten shekels of silver by the year, and a suit of apparel, and thy victuals. evidence.title: Ezra 7:12 (the king’s greeting) — “perfect peace” against “let the word and the answer be completed”
evidence.summary: Ezra 7:12 in the KJV greets Ezra with “perfect peace, and at such a time”. The old Greek translation asks that the word and answer be completed. The source language of this verse is Aramaic.
evidence.text: KJV Ezra 7:12: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, unto Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, perfect peace, and at such a time.” Aramaic text Ezra 7:12: אַ֨רְתַּחְשַׁ֔סְתְּא מֶ֖לֶךְ מַלְכַיָּ֑א לְעֶזְרָ֣א כָ֠הֲנָא סָפַ֨ר דָּתָ֜א דִּֽי־אֱלָ֧הּ שְׁמַיָּ֛א גְּמִ֖יר וּכְעֶֽנֶת׃ [Aramaic rendering: complete, and now.] Old Greek translation Ezra 7:12: Ἀρθασασθὰ βασιλεὺς βασιλέων Ἔσδρᾳ γραμματεῖ νόμου Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ· τετελέσθω λόγος καὶ ἡ ἀπόκρισις. [Greek rendering: let a word and the answer be completed.]
evidence.reasoning: The KJV presents a greeting of peace, while this Greek wording presents a request for completion. The Aramaic text does not include a word for peace.

evidence.title: Ezra 7:26 (the king’s penalties) — “banishment” against “chastisement”
evidence.summary: Ezra 7:26 in the KJV lists death, banishment, loss of goods and imprisonment. The old Greek translation uses chastisement, or corrective punishment, as its second item. Both lists have four items.
evidence.text: KJV Ezra 7:26: “And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether it be unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment.” Aramaic text Ezra 7:26: וְכָל־דִּי־לָא֩ לֶהֱוֵ֨א עָבֵ֜ד דָּתָ֣א דִֽי־אֱלָהָ֗ךְ וְדָתָא֙ דִּ֣י מַלְכָּ֔א אָסְפַּ֕רְנָא דִּינָ֕ה לֶהֱוֵ֥א מִתְעֲבֵ֖ד מִנֵּ֑הּ הֵ֤ן לְמֹות֙ הֵ֣ן [לִשְׁרֹשׁוּ כ] (לִשְׁרֹשִׁ֔י ק) הֵן־לַעֲנָ֥שׁ נִכְסִ֖ין וְלֶאֱסוּרִֽין׃  פ [Aramaic: the text marks separate forms to write and to read; their meaning is not settled here.] Old Greek translation Ezra 7:26: Καὶ πὰς ὃς ἂν μὴ ᾖ ποιῶν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ νόμον τοῦ βασιλέως ἑτοίμως, τὸ κρίμα ἔσται γινόμενον ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ἐάν τε εἰς θάνατον, ἐάν τε εἰς παιδείαν, ἐάν τε εἰς ζημίαν τοῦ βίου. ἐάν τε εἰς παράδοσιν. [Greek rendering: to death, to chastisement, to loss of property, to delivery.]
evidence.reasoning: The comparison is banishment versus corrective punishment in the second position. The Greek does not add an extra penalty.

evidence.title: Ezra 9:13–14 — “punished us less than our iniquities deserve” and a question of anger, against “there is none such as our God” and a plea

evidence.title: God Named in Five Greek Passages of Esther
evidence.summary: The old Greek translation names God in five places where the KJV and Hebrew text do not. Mordecai tells Esther to fear God at 2:20 and call on the Lord at 4:8. At 6:1, the Lord removes the king’s sleep. At 6:13, Haman hears that a living God is with Mordecai. At Greek 5:1e, God changes the king’s spirit to gentleness; the paired KJV passage is 5:2. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV’s Esther finds no God, gods or Lord, in any letter case.
evidence.text: KJV Esther 6:1: “On that night could not the king sleep” Hebrew text: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ [in that night the sleep of the king fled]. Old Greek translation: Ὁ δε Κύριος ἀπέστησε τὸν ὕπνον ἀπὸ τοὺ βασιλέως τὴν νύκτα ἐκείνην [but the Lord removed sleep from the king that night]. KJV Esther 2:20: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” Hebrew: וְאֶת־מַאֲמַ֤ר מָרְדֳּכַי֙ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עֹשָׂ֔ה [and the command of Mordecai Esther did]. Greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἐνετείλατο αὐτῇ Μαρδοχαῖος, φοβεῖσθαι τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ ποιεῖν τὰ προστάγματα αὐτοῦ [for so Mardochaeus commanded her, to fear God and to do his commandments]. KJV Esther 4:8: “to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people” Hebrew: וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל־עַמָּֽהּ [and to make request before him for her people], the last words of the verse. Greek, continuing after the matching words: ἐπικάλεσαι τὸν Κύριον, καὶ λάλησον τῷ βασιλεῖ περὶ ἡμῶν, ῥύσαι ἡμᾶς ἐκ θανάτου. [call upon the Lord, and speak to the king about us, to deliver us from death]. KJV Esther 6:13: “thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him” Hebrew: כִּֽי־נָפֹ֥ול תִּפֹּ֖ול לְפָנָֽיו [but falling thou shalt fall before him], the last words of the verse. Greek: καὶ οὐ μὴ δύνῃ αὐτὸν ἀμύνασθαι, ὅτι Θεὸς ζῶν μετʼ αὐτοῦ. [and thou shalt not be able to withstand him, because a living God is with him]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG06.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG02.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG04.htm. KJV Esther 5:2: “she obtained favour in his sight” Hebrew text Esther 5:2: נָשְׂאָ֥ה חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינָ֑יו [she carried favour in his eyes]. Old Greek translation Esther 5:1e: Καὶ μετέβαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ βασιλέως εἰς πραύτητα, καὶ ἀγωνιάσας ἀνεπήδησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὰς ἀγκάλας αὐτοῦ, μέχρις οὗ κατέστη· καὶ παρεκάλει αὐτὴν λόγοις εἰρηνικοῖς [And God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and in alarm he leapt from his throne and took her in his arms until she stood, and comforted her with peaceful words]. evidence.summary: Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4 appeal to Jerusalem's daughters. The KJV gives no basis for these oaths. The old Greek translation adds powers and forces of the field at 5:8. It adds forces of the field at 8:4.

Sources name the Hebrew text and the old Greek translation used here. English in square brackets is the researcher’s rendering, not KJV wording or a dictionary definition.

evidence.title: Jehu paying tribute to Shalmaneser III (Black Obelisk)
evidence.summary: The Black Obelisk caption lists tribute from Jehu, son of Omri. He is usually identified with the king in 2 Kings 9–10. Those chapters describe Jehu ending Ahab's house and Hazael taking Israel's eastern lands. They do not report this tribute. A separate Assyrian account places the tribute in Shalmaneser III's eighteenth year, usually dated to 841 BCE.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Kings 10:11: “So Jehu slew all that remained of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, and all his great men, and his kinsfolks, and his priests, until he left him none remaining.”
evidence.reasoning: The caption lists silver, gold, gold vessels, lead, staves and javelins. The separate account of the king's deeds names tribute from Tyre, Sidon and Jehu after fighting Hazael. These are two distinct passages in Luckenbill's edition. The usual reading treats son of Omri as a label for the kingdom, not proof of Jehu's descent. The compared Kings account instead has Jehu destroy Ahab's house.
evidence.scope: The date of about 841 BCE applies to the reported tribute, not the making of the obelisk. The identification of Jehu and the kingdom-label reading remain usual interpretations. They do not prove a family link to Omri. The silence claim concerns only the compared account in 2 Kings 9–10. Its silence does not disprove the tribute. The cited Assyrian passages do not describe Jehu's coup. The later museum article checks the older translation; no new reading of the ancient signs is claimed.

sources.label: Luckenbill (1926), Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia, vol. 1, sections 590 (Black Obelisk relief caption) and 672 (annals, year 18) (Internet Archive scan, opened)
Tammi Schneider, Through Assyria’s Eyes, Penn Museum: Jehu, the eighteenth year and the Omri label

evidence.title: Esarhaddon and Manasseh of Judah
evidence.summary: Esarhaddon's palace-building list names Manasseh king of Judah among rulers required to send materials. This demand suggests that Judah was under Assyrian rule. It is an inference from the list. In 2 Kings 21:1–2, Manasseh begins ruling at twelve, reigns fifty-five years and does evil. In 2 Chronicles 33:11–13, Assyrians take him to Babylon. The account says he humbles himself and returns to Jerusalem.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Chronicles 33:11: “Wherefore the Lord brought upon them the captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.”
evidence.reasoning: The list begins with Baal of Tyre, Manasseh of Judah, Kaushgabri of Edom and Musuri of Moab. Rogers's translation and the later translation in Sources describe the demand and transport of building materials. The list does not mention Manasseh's capture, journey to Babylon or return. That silence neither proves nor disproves the Chronicles account. Kings and Chronicles report different details; this comparison does not rank their reliability.
evidence.scope: Chronicles does not name the Assyrian king who takes Manasseh. This record does not identify him as Esarhaddon. The quotation uses the packaged KJV's among the thorns; no alternative word meaning is established. The claim about Assyrian control rests on an inference from the demand for materials. The later translation is a check on Rogers, not a fresh reading of the tablet.

sources.label: Rogers (1912), Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, Esarhaddon introduction (pp. 349-350) and Prism B, col. V, lines 12-23 (Internet Archive scan, opened)
A. Leo Oppenheim, Esarhaddon’s Prism B, ANET third edition, translated text hosted by Livius

evidence.title: Merodach-baladan and Hezekiah
evidence.summary: Kings and Isaiah describe a Babylonian king sending letters and a gift after hearing that Hezekiah had been ill. The KJV names him Berodachbaladan in 2 Kings 20:12 and Merodachbaladan in Isaiah 39:1. Kings says Hezekiah hearkened to the visitors; Isaiah says he was glad of them. Isaiah also says Hezekiah had recovered. A Babylonian chronicle records Merodach-baladan's reign, but does not report this embassy.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Kings 20:12: “At that time Berodachbaladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah: for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick.”
evidence.reasoning: The chronicle names Merodach-baladan, also called Marduk-apal-iddin, as king of Babylon. He is generally identified with the king in Kings and Isaiah. It records his accession, twelve-year reign and flight to Elam after Sargon fights him. It also reports later conflict under Sennacherib. These events support the reign setting, not an embassy date or motive. In 2 Chronicles 32:31, the visitors ask about a wonder in the land. That account says God left Hezekiah to test him.
evidence.scope: The compared biblical passages give no year for the embassy. This record does not choose between the king's first and later reign. It makes no claim about a KJV margin. The English names are the spellings in the packaged KJV. The Hebrew names differ in more than their first letter: Kings also includes a letter absent from Isaiah. The two Hebrew verbs also differ. No quoted Latin form is presented as exact Hebrew. The chronicle neither confirms nor contradicts the embassy, and does not establish its motive.

evidence.title: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Egypt (567 BCE)
evidence.summary: A damaged Babylonian text reports a campaign against Egypt in Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year. The usual date is 568/567 BCE. The Egyptian king's name is partly restored as Amasis. Ezekiel and Jeremiah predict Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Egypt. This is a proposed comparison with those passages. They are predictions, not reports of the campaign.
evidence.text: KJV Ezekiel 29:19: “Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall take her multitude, and take her spoil, and take her prey; and it shall be the wages for his army.”
evidence.reasoning: Ezekiel 29:17–20 dates its message to the twenty-seventh year. It presents Egypt as payment for the army's work against Tyre. Ezekiel 30:10–12 and Jeremiah 43:8–13 and 46:13 also predict an attack on Egypt. Rogers's translation describes troops and battle, with gaps in the text. His tentative fragments about defeat and destruction do not establish conquest. The later transcription also keeps gaps and partly restores the king's name. It supports the limited campaign notice.
evidence.scope: The broken text does not establish that Egypt was conquered, taken or made a province. It does not settle whether the predictions were fulfilled or failed. A missing or unclear result cannot decide that question. The newer author draws wider conclusions about history. This record does not adopt them. The existing Tyre record compares biblical passages internally. This History record concerns only the Egypt fragment and its proposed link with these texts. The date belongs to the reported campaign, not a date stated in the prophetic passages.

sources.label: Rogers (1912), Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Nebuchadrezzar's Campaign against Egypt (567 B.C.)', text and translation of the British Museum fragment (Internet Archive scan, opened)
Aren M. Wilson-Wright, Jeremiah’s Egypt, pp. 31–32: fragmentary campaign text and restored name

evidence.title: Mesha And Israel’s Rule
evidence.summary: Kings links Moab’s revolt with Ahab’s death. Mesha’s stone describes Moab regaining land held by Israel. Both concern conflict between these kingdoms. This comparison does not establish that they describe the same stage of that conflict.
evidence.reasoning: The Louvre identifies the stone as a record of Mesha’s victories. Its date fields differ within the ninth century BCE. The cited translation mentions Omri’s son and forty years. Those details need review before matching the accounts year by year.
evidence.scope: A royal victory record gives one ruler’s account. It does not independently confirm every event in Kings. This draft assigns no precise year. It does not identify the unnamed son or resolve the forty years.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Kings 3:5: “But it came to pass, when Ahab was dead, that the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.”

sources.label: Louvre, Mesha stone AO 5066
K. C. Hanson, Mesha translation adapted from Albright

evidence.title: Kings And The Karnak Place List
evidence.summary: Kings describes an Egyptian campaign against Jerusalem. A survey records the Bubastite Portal at Karnak and its list of conquered places. The list offers a separate ancient source to compare with Kings. Each proposed place match needs its own review.
evidence.reasoning: The survey documents the surviving relief and inscriptions. It supplies primary material for later checks of the campaign’s reach. It does not make every old place reading certain. The earlier draft’s detailed geography is held for further review.
evidence.scope: This draft does not settle the identity of each place or assign a precise campaign year. It does not infer Jerusalem’s fate from a missing name. The earlier city list remains outside this draft.
evidence.text: KJV 1 Kings 14:25: “And it came to pass in the fifth year of king Rehoboam, that Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem:”

evidence.title: Samaria In Kings And Sargon’s Account
evidence.summary: Kings reports Samaria’s capture by the king of Assyria. Sargon’s inscription also claims the city’s capture and removal of people. This gives an outside royal claim about Samaria. The relationship between these accounts still needs a chronology review.
evidence.reasoning: The current edition prints 27,290 people in one copy. Its notes record different totals in other copies. The account names Sargon as the speaker. Kings names Shalmaneser earlier in the campaign, then refers to the king of Assyria.
evidence.scope: A claim by Sargon does not settle who first captured the city. Differing copies limit the precision of the total. This draft does not force the two campaigns into one year. It does not turn royal claims into independently verified counts.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Kings 17:6: “In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.”

evidence.title: Judah In An Assyrian Tribute List
evidence.summary: Kings describes Ahaz sending silver and gold to the king of Assyria. An Assyrian list names Jehoahaz of Judah among rulers sending goods. The passages offer a comparison about payments to Assyria. This draft leaves the name match open.
evidence.reasoning: The current edition preserves the name Jehoahaz beside Judah. Parts of the surrounding payment list are damaged. The surviving name can guide a comparison with Kings. It does not alone explain the payment’s purpose or establish every proposed identity.
evidence.scope: This draft covers the tribute list only. It does not settle Pul’s identity or who killed Pekah. It does not assume that a longer name proves an identity. The broader draft remains held for those source checks.
evidence.text: KJV 2 Kings 16:8: “And Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the house of the Lord, and in the treasures of the king's house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.”

people.name: Jethro
people.summary: The priest of Midian whose daughter Zipporah marries Moses. Exodus says he gives Moses refuge and releases him to return to Egypt. He later brings Moses' wife and sons to the camp at the mountain of God. He praises the Lord after hearing of Israel's escape from Egypt and offers sacrifices. He advises Moses to appoint officials to share the work of judging the people. Exodus uses Jethro and Reuel; Numbers 10:29 uses Raguel. These name links do not settle Hobab's relationship to Moses.

children: Seven daughters in all (Exodus 2:16; only Zipporah is named)

residence: The camp at the mountain of God (Exodus 18:5)

people.name: Zipporah
people.summary: A daughter of the Midianite priest who becomes Moses' wife and bears Gershom and Eliezer. On the journey, she circumcises her son after the Lord threatens a man's life. Exodus 4:24 uses “him” without naming the man. She uses a sharp stone and speaks of a “bloody husband”. Exodus 18:2 says Moses had sent her back but does not say when. Her father brings her and her sons to Moses at the mountain of God.

residence: Her father's house after being sent back (Exodus 18:2)
The camp at the mountain of God (Exodus 18:5)

people.name: Eleazar
people.summary: Aaron's third-named son, who becomes high priest after his two older brothers and Aaron die. Numbers places Aaron's death on Mount Hor, where Moses puts Aaron's garments on Eleazar. He works with Moses during the census and the war against Midian. Later, he helps divide the land with Joshua.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained
Edom Refuses Passage and Aaron Dies
A New Census and Joshua Appointed

people.name: Phinehas
people.summary: Eleazar's son. Numbers describes an Israelite bringing a Midianite woman into the camp during a plague at Shittim. Phinehas takes a javelin and kills them both. In the account, the Lord says he turned away wrath. The Lord promises him peace and a lasting priesthood. He later carries sacred objects during the war against Midian. He leads the group sent to the eastern tribes during the altar dispute.

people.name: Caleb
people.summary: Jephunneh's son, whom Numbers calls a Kenezite and a man of Judah. He is one of twelve men sent to spy out Canaan and urges Israel to go up at once. He and Joshua tear their clothes when the people refuse. Numbers says he survives the wilderness generation because he followed the Lord fully. At eighty-five, he asks for the hill country of Hebron and drives out the sons of Anak. This profile does not identify him with the Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:18.

geography.origin: A Kenezite of the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6; Numbers 32:12)
residence: Sent from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land (Joshua 14:7)

linked_stories.title: Tribes Settle East of the Jordan

people.name: Korah
people.summary: A Levite from Kohath's family and a son of Izhar. In Numbers 16, he gathers followers with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders against Moses and Aaron. They say the whole community is holy. The account describes the earth swallowing Korah's company and fire consuming the 250 who offered incense. Numbers 26:11 says Korah's children did not die. These accounts are not combined into a more detailed death sequence here.

geography.origin: A Levite, son of Izhar, son of Kohath (Numbers 16:1)
residence: The wilderness camp, near the tabernacle (Numbers 16:19)

people.name: Balaam
people.summary: Beor's son from Pethor, whom Balak king of Moab calls to curse Israel. Numbers describes an angel and a speaking donkey before Balaam is allowed to go. From Moab's heights he blesses Israel instead, including a message about a star from Jacob. Numbers 31 links him to Israel's actions at Peor and says Israel killed him in the war against Midian. Second Peter and Revelation also criticize him.

geography.origin: Pethor, by the river of his people (Numbers 22:5)
residence: The heights of Moab overlooking Israel (Numbers 22:41)

people.name: Balak
people.summary: The son of Zippor and king of Moab, alarmed by Israel's defeat of the Amorites and its numbers. He sends for Balaam to curse Israel and takes him to a series of high places. Each message blesses Israel instead. Numbers 24:10 describes Balak's anger.

people.name: Nadab
people.summary: Aaron's firstborn son, who goes up the mountain with Moses and Aaron. Exodus says they see the God of Israel. Nadab is appointed a priest. Leviticus says he and Abihu offer fire the Lord had not commanded, and fire from the Lord consumes them. Numbers says they die without children.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained

people.name: Abihu
people.summary: Aaron's second-named son, who goes up the mountain with Moses. Exodus says they see the God of Israel. He is appointed a priest. Leviticus says he and Nadab offer uncommanded fire in incense holders and die before the Lord.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; named among Aaron's sons in Exodus 6:23.

linked_stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained

people.name: Hur
people.summary: A man who stands with Aaron during the battle with Amalek and helps hold up Moses' hands until sunset. When Moses goes up the mountain, he leaves Hur with Aaron to settle disputes. Exodus 31:2 names a Hur as Bezaleel's grandfather. It does not establish that this is the same Hur.

geography.origin: Birthplace and tribe not stated in the cited Exodus account.
residence: The camp, while Moses is on the mountain (Exodus 24:14)

linked_stories.title: Water from the Rock and the Battle with Amalek

people.name: Bezaleel
people.summary: A craftsman from Judah, son of Uri and grandson of Hur. Exodus says the Lord calls him by name and fills him with God's spirit, wisdom and skill. With Aholiab of Dan, he makes the sacred tent, its furnishings and the priests' garments as commanded.

geography.origin: Tribe of Judah, son of Uri, son of Hur (Exodus 31:2)

people.name: Rahab
people.summary: A woman of Jericho whom Joshua describes as a sex worker. She hides two spies on her roof, misleads the king's men and lowers the spies through her window. She says fear of Israel has fallen on the land and asks for kindness to her father's household. Joshua says she and her family survive Jericho's fall, and she lives among Israel. Matthew names Rachab in its family list; Hebrews and James also name Rahab. These later references do not establish every proposed family link here.

residence: A house on the town wall of Jericho (Joshua 2:15)

people.name: Achan
people.summary: A man of Judah who takes goods set apart at Jericho: a garment, silver and gold. He hides them in his tent, and Israel later loses at Ai. Joshua describes groups being selected until Achan is singled out. He admits wanting and taking the goods. The account describes stoning and burning in the valley of Achor. Its pronouns are not used here to settle exactly who or what is burned.

residence: Israel's camp at Jericho and Ai (Joshua 7:1)
Valley of Achor, where he is buried under stones (Joshua 7:26)

people.name: Othniel
people.summary: Kenaz's son, who captures a town and receives Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife. The phrase “younger brother” can refer to Kenaz or Othniel; this profile does not choose between them. Judges says Israel cries out under Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia. The Lord raises Othniel as a deliverer, and the Lord's spirit comes on him. The account gives the land forty years of rest until his death.

geography.origin: Not stated beyond his family of Kenaz (Judges 3:9)

people.name: Ehud
people.summary: A left-handed man of Benjamin and son of Gera. Judges says the Lord raises him when Israel cries out under Eglon king of Moab. He brings tribute to Eglon, then returns to kill him with a dagger and escapes. He rallies Israel, which defeats Moab. Judges gives the land eighty years of rest. This profile does not identify him with the other Ehud in Chronicles.

people.name: Deborah
people.summary: A prophet and the wife of Lapidoth who judges Israel beneath a palm tree in Ephraim's hill country. She calls Barak to lead ten thousand men against Sisera and agrees to go with him. Judges records her warning that the Lord will give Sisera into a woman's hand. Judges 5:1 names Deborah and Barak as singers of the victory song. This Deborah is distinct from Rebekah's nurse.

geography.origin: Not stated; she held court in the hill country of Ephraim (Judges 4:5)
residence: Under the palm tree of Deborah, between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:5)

people.name: Barak
people.summary: Abinoam's son from Kedesh-naphtali, called by Deborah to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor against Sisera. He insists that she go with him. She warns that the honour of victory will pass to a woman. He pursues Sisera and finds him dead in Jael's tent. Hebrews 11:32 later names Barak among people it praises for faith.

residence: Mount Tabor, where he musters the army (Judges 4:6)

people.name: Jael
people.summary: The wife of Heber the Kenite. Judges says Sisera flees to her tent after his army's defeat, since Jabin and Heber's household are at peace. She welcomes him and drives a tent nail through his temples while he sleeps. She shows Barak the dead man. The song in Judges 5 blesses her above women in tents.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; she lives in Heber's tent in Judges 4:17.

people.name: Gideon
people.summary: Joash's son, an Abiezrite from Manasseh. Judges describes an angel calling him to save Israel while he threshes wheat in a winepress. He asks for a sign with a fleece. He reduces his army to three hundred and defeats Midian with trumpets and torches in jars. He refuses to rule but makes an ephod, an object used in worship whose precise form is not given. Judges calls it a trap for Israel and his household. The text lists seventy sons, then introduces Abimelech separately; no revised total is supplied here.

children: Abimelech, by a concubine at Shechem

people.name: Abimelech
people.summary: Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem, a partner distinct from a wife. His mother's relatives support his claim to rule. Judges 9:5 says he kills seventy brothers on one stone, while also saying Jotham survives. The people make him king at Shechem. Judges says God sends an evil spirit between him and Shechem's men. He destroys the city. At Thebez, a woman breaks his skull with a millstone. The text calls his death God's repayment for his wickedness.

siblings: Seventy brothers in Judges 9:5, which also says Jotham survived

people.name: Jephthah
people.summary: A warrior from Gilead, whose parents are Gilead and a woman the text calls a harlot. The elders call him back to lead against Ammon. Judges says the Lord's spirit comes on him. He vows, or promises, to offer whoever first leaves his house to greet him as a burnt offering. His only daughter comes out first. The text says he acts according to his vow; this profile does not settle sacrifice versus dedication. He later fights Ephraim at the Jordan crossings and judges Israel for six years.

people.name: Samson
people.summary: Manoah's son from Dan, announced as set apart for God from birth. Judges says he will begin to free Israel from the Philistines. He marries a Philistine woman from Timnath, kills many Philistines and judges Israel for twenty years. Samson tells Delilah that shaving his hair will take away his strength. Judges 16:20 also says the Lord has left him. He is shaved, blinded and made to grind in Gaza's prison. At the Philistine temple, he asks to die with them and brings the building down.

geography.origin: Zorah, of the family of the Danites (Judges 13:2)

people.name: Delilah
people.summary: A woman Samson loves in the valley of Sorek. Judges 16 says the Philistine rulers ask her to draw out the source of his strength. She presses him until he tells her. She lets him sleep on her knees and calls a man to shave his seven locks. The account says his strength then leaves him. It does not give her birthplace or ethnic identity.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; the account places her in the valley of Sorek (Judges 16:4).

people.name: Naomi
people.summary: Elimelech's wife from Bethlehem, who moves to Moab during a famine. There she loses her husband and her sons Mahlon and Chilion. She returns to Bethlehem with her daughter-in-law Ruth. She asks to be called Mara, saying the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. She guides Ruth toward Boaz. When Obed is born, the neighbours say a son is born to Naomi. Their words in Ruth 4:17 do not make Naomi his birth mother.

linked_stories.title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem

people.name: Ruth
people.summary: A Moabite woman who marries Mahlon, Naomi's son. After his death, she stays with Naomi and says Naomi's people and God will be hers. In Bethlehem, she gathers grain left by harvesters in the field of Boaz, a relative. Following Naomi's advice, she asks him to act as a close relative at the threshing floor. The account describes the nearer relative declining the family and land arrangement. Boaz marries her, and she bears Obed, Jesse's father and David's grandfather. Matthew names her in its family list.

linked_stories.title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem

people.name: Boaz
people.summary: A wealthy relative of Elimelech in Bethlehem who lets Ruth gather grain left in his field. At the threshing floor, she asks him to spread his skirt over her as a close relative. He arranges to buy the family land at the town gate. He marries Ruth to preserve the dead man's name through his inheritance. Their son Obed is Jesse's father. Matthew names Booz as the son of Salmon and Rachab. That family list does not itself settle further claims about Rachab's identity.

people.name: Hannah
people.summary: One of Elkanah's two wives from Ramathaim-zophim. She has no children, and Peninnah taunts her. At Shiloh, Eli first mistakes her intense prayer for drunkenness. She promises to give a son to the Lord. She bears Samuel and brings him to Shiloh after he stops nursing, leaving him there to serve. First Samuel 2 opens with her prayer of praise. The account later gives her three more sons and two daughters.

children: Three more sons and two daughters (unnamed; 1 Samuel 2:21)

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

people.name: Eli
people.summary: The priest at Shiloh who watches Hannah pray and later trains the child Samuel. First Samuel calls his sons Hophni and Phinehas “sons of Belial”, a harsh description of their wrongdoing. They misuse their office. Eli rebukes them but does not stop them. An unnamed man of God warns of judgment on Eli's family. The account later describes the Lord giving Samuel a similar warning. At ninety-eight, Eli hears that the ark is taken and his sons are dead. He falls from his seat and dies. The text says he judged Israel forty years.

geography.origin: Shiloh, where he sits at the temple of the Lord (1 Samuel 1:9)

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

people.name: Samuel
people.summary: Elkanah and Hannah's son, given to serve the Lord at Shiloh under Eli. First Samuel describes the Lord calling him as a child. The text presents him as a prophet known from Dan to Beersheba. He judges Israel on a yearly circuit and lives at Ramah. He anoints Saul as leader and later anoints David among his brothers. He rebukes Saul, saying obedience is better than sacrifice. The book covers the end of the judges and the start of the kingdom. It says Samuel judged Israel throughout his life.

linked_stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel

people.name: Saul
people.summary: Kish's son from Benjamin, described as taller than any other man in Israel. Samuel anoints him, and he becomes Israel's first king. He fights the Philistines. Samuel says the Lord has rejected him as king for failing to keep the Lord's word. David enters his service. First Samuel 18:8–12 describes Saul's anger and fear; the later account follows his pursuit of David. When the Lord no longer answers, he consults a medium at Endor. Archers wound him on Mount Gilboa, and he falls on his sword. Jonathan and two other sons die that day.

residence: Mount Gilboa, where he dies (1 Samuel 31:1)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

people.name: Jonathan
people.summary: Saul's son and David's friend. He and his armour carrier attack a Philistine outpost without telling Saul. The people later refuse to let Saul put Jonathan to death. He and David make a lasting agreement. Jonathan gives David his robe, sword and bow and warns him of Saul's plans. He says David will be king, with himself next in rank. He dies with Saul at Gilboa. David's song of grief calls Jonathan's love wonderful.

residence: Gibeah, in his father's house (1 Samuel 14:2)
Mount Gilboa, where he dies (1 Samuel 31:2)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

people.name: David
people.summary: Jesse's youngest son from Bethlehem, summoned from the sheep and then anointed by Samuel. He kills Goliath with a sling and stone and serves Saul. He later flees Saul, leading an outlaw group in the wilderness and at Ziklag. After Saul's death, he becomes king at Hebron. The account gives him seven and a half years there and thirty-three in Jerusalem. It describes the Lord promising him a lasting royal line and throne. Nathan confronts him over Bathsheba and Uriah's death. The book also describes Absalom's revolt. The New Testament names David in Jesus' family list and Paul's speech at Antioch.

geography.origin: Bethlehem of Judah, son of Jesse (1 Samuel 17:12)
residence: The cave Adullam and the wilderness (1 Samuel 22:1)
Jerusalem, the city of David (2 Samuel 5:7)

linked_stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death

people.name: Michal
people.summary: Saul's younger daughter, who loves David. Saul gives her to David after he brings back two hundred Philistine foreskins. When Saul sends men to kill David, she lowers David through a window. He escapes. Saul later gives her to Phalti son of Laish. David demands her return through Abner and Ishbosheth. When the ark enters Jerusalem, she sees David dancing and despises him in her heart. Second Samuel 6:23 says she had no child until her death. This profile does not settle that statement against 2 Samuel 21:8.

residence: The house of David in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:16)

people.name: Abigail
people.summary: Nabal's wife from Carmel, whom First Samuel describes as having good understanding. Nabal is described as harsh. After he insults David's men, Abigail brings David bread, wine, sheep, grain, raisins and figs without telling Nabal. About ten days later, Nabal dies. David then sends for Abigail, and she becomes his wife. Second Samuel 3:3 names their son Chileab; the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 3:1 names him Daniel.

geography.origin: Carmel, the home of Nabal (1 Samuel 25:3)

people.name: Bathsheba
people.summary: Eliam's daughter and Uriah the Hittite's wife in Second Samuel. First Chronicles' parallel family list uses the names Bathshua and Ammiel; the name link is not proved here. David sees Bathsheba from his roof, sends for her and has sex with her. She conceives; David arranges Uriah's death and marries her. Their first child dies. She later bears Solomon, whom the text says the Lord loved. With Nathan, she raises the succession with the ageing David, who promises Solomon the throne. Solomon later seats her at his right hand. Matthew calls her the wife of Urias.

geography.origin: Not stated; daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3)

people.name: Nathan
people.summary: A prophet at David's court, distinct from David's son of that name. In Second Samuel 7, he first supports David's plan for a house for the ark. He changes his answer after receiving the Lord's word. He tells David about a rich man taking a poor man's lamb, then says, “Thou art the man”. David confesses, and Nathan says the Lord has put away his sin. The name Jedidiah is given to the child through Nathan. Later, Nathan joins Bathsheba in urging David to make Solomon king. David directs Nathan and Zadok to anoint Solomon.

people.name: Absalom
people.summary: David's third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, the daughter of Geshur's king. Second Samuel praises his beauty. He has Amnon killed after Amnon rapes his sister Tamar, then flees to Geshur for three years. Joab brings him back. He wins over people seeking the king's judgment and proclaims himself king at Hebron. David leaves Jerusalem. Absalom catches his head in an oak and is killed by Joab and ten armour carriers. David mourns him with “O my son Absalom”. The account names three sons and a daughter; this profile does not settle that against 2 Samuel 18:18.

children: Three sons (unnamed) and a daughter, Tamar

residence: Geshur, with his mother's father (2 Samuel 13:38)
Hebron, where he is proclaimed king (2 Samuel 15:10)

people.name: Joab
people.summary: Zeruiah's son, brother of Abishai and Asahel, and commander of David's army. Second Samuel says he kills Abner to avenge Asahel. He later kills Amasa and strikes Absalom with darts against David's wishes. David calls Zeruiah's sons too hard for him. Joab supports Adonijah in the struggle for the throne; he had not supported Absalom. Following David's charge, Solomon orders Benaiah to kill Joab beside the altar. Joab is buried at his own house in the wilderness.

geography.origin: Not stated; his brother Asahel is buried at Bethlehem (2 Samuel 2:32)
residence: Camp and campaign for David (2 Samuel 8:16)
The tabernacle of the Lord, where he catches the altar's horns (1 Kings 2:28)

people.name: Solomon
people.summary: David and Bathsheba's son, also given the name Jedidiah because of the Lord. He becomes king after David, despite Adonijah's attempt to take the throne. He asks God for understanding to judge the people. The account says God gives him wisdom and further gifts he did not request. He builds the temple over seven years. Kings lists seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, partners distinct from wives. It says his heart turns toward other gods in old age. It gives him forty years as king in Jerusalem.

geography.origin: Jerusalem, born to David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:24)

linked_stories.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Decline

people.name: Mephibosheth
people.summary: Jonathan's son, whose feet are disabled after his nurse drops him while fleeing when he is five. David restores Saul's land to him and gives him a place at the king's table for Jonathan's sake. During Absalom's revolt, Ziba says Mephibosheth stayed behind hoping to gain the kingdom. David gives Ziba his goods. On David's return, Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him. David tells them to divide the land; Mephibosheth says Ziba can take it all. This profile does not decide between their accounts. A parallel family list uses Meribbaal; he is distinct from the Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel 21:8.

residence: Lo-debar, before David summoned him (2 Samuel 9:4)
Jerusalem, eating at the king's table (2 Samuel 9:13)

people.name: Uriah
people.summary: Bathsheba's husband, called a Hittite and listed among David's thirty-seven leading warriors. David orders Joab to place him where the battle is fiercest and withdraw so he will be killed. Uriah dies during the siege. Joab's message anticipates David's anger. Matthew refers to him as Urias. The Hittite label does not establish his birthplace.

geography.origin: Not stated; called a Hittite (2 Samuel 11:3)
residence: Jerusalem, near the king's house (2 Samuel 11:3)
The siege of Rabbah, where he dies (2 Samuel 11:17)

people.name: Rehoboam
people.summary: Solomon's son by Naamah the Ammonite, who becomes king at Shechem at forty-one. The people ask him to ease the burdens Solomon imposed. He rejects the elders' advice for that of his young peers. He promises “scorpions” where Solomon used whips. Ten tribes leave him, while Judah and Benjamin remain. Kings says a message through Shemaiah stops him from attacking Israel. In his fifth year, Shishak of Egypt takes treasures from the temple and royal house. War with Jeroboam continues throughout his reign.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:21).

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

people.name: Jeroboam
people.summary: Nebat and Zeruah's son from Zereda, called an Ephrathite. Solomon puts him over the labour force of Joseph's tribes. Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces and gives him ten, with a conditional promise of a lasting royal line. Solomon seeks to kill him, so he flees to Egypt until Solomon dies. The people call him back and make him king at Shechem. He sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, appoints priests outside Levi and establishes an eighth-month feast. Kings uses his sin to judge later rulers. He reigns twenty-two years, followed by his son Nadab.

residence: Shechem, which he built in mount Ephraim (1 Kings 12:25)
Egypt, in flight from Solomon (1 Kings 11:40)

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

people.name: Ahab
people.summary: Omri's son, who rules Israel from Samaria for twenty-two years. Kings says he does more evil than all before him. He marries Jezebel, Ethbaal's daughter, and serves Baal. Elijah announces a drought, meets him on Carmel and confronts him after Naboth's death. Ahab then humbles himself. While fighting Syria at Ramoth-gilead, an arrow shot at random strikes him. Kings says he dies that evening in his chariot and dogs lick the blood washed from it. This profile does not settle Athaliah's parentage or identify Ahab with Jeremiah's Ahab.

children: Daughter, wife of Jehoram of Judah (2 Kings 8:18)

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Samaria (1 Kings 16:29).
residence: Jezreel, where Naboth's vineyard lay (1 Kings 21:1)

people.name: Jezebel
people.summary: Ethbaal's daughter and Ahab's wife. Kings says Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal. It describes her killing the Lord's prophets and supporting four hundred prophets of the groves. She threatens Elijah's life after Carmel. Using letters sealed with Ahab's seal, she arranges false charges against Naboth and his death by stoning. When Jehu reaches Jezreel, she paints her face and looks from a window. Court servants throw her down, and she is trampled. Only her skull, feet and palms remain when people come to bury her. Jehu links this to Elijah's words about dogs eating her flesh.

people.name: Jehu
people.summary: Son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, serving as a commander at Ramoth-gilead. A prophet sent by Elisha anoints him king of Israel. He shoots Joram at Naboth's plot, orders Ahaziah struck down and sees Jezebel thrown from her window. He has Ahab's seventy sons killed at Samaria and destroys Baal's worshippers and temple. Kings describes the Lord promising his descendants four generations on the throne. It also criticizes his continued calf worship and incomplete obedience. He reigns twenty-eight years. His father's name does not identify him with King Jehoshaphat of Judah.

geography.origin: Ramoth-gilead, as captain among the host (2 Kings 9:1)

people.name: Athaliah
people.summary: Ahaziah of Judah's mother. Second Kings 8:26 calls her Omri's daughter; 8:18 calls Jehoram's wife Ahab's daughter. These labels do not settle the exact family relationship here. After Ahaziah dies, she attacks the royal family. Jehosheba, Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, hides the infant Joash in the temple for six years while Athaliah rules. In the seventh year, Jehoiada makes an agreement with the captains and guards and crowns Joash. Athaliah is taken out and killed near the horses' entrance to the royal house.

geography.origin: Israel, daughter of the house of Omri (2 Kings 8:26)

people.name: Naaman
people.summary: A Syrian commander whom Second Kings describes as honoured and brave, but affected by leprosy. A captive Israelite girl tells his wife about the prophet in Samaria. Naaman travels with his king's letter. Elisha tells him to wash seven times in the Jordan. He is angry, but follows his servants' advice and washes. The account says he is healed. He declares that God is found only in Israel and takes earth home for worship. He asks pardon for bowing in Rimmon's temple while attending his master. Jesus mentions Naaman while discussing lepers in Israel during Elisha's time.

geography.origin: Syria, captain of the host of its king (2 Kings 5:1)
residence: The Jordan, where he washes (2 Kings 5:14)

people.name: Hezekiah
people.summary: Ahaz and Abi's son, who becomes Judah's king at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years. He removes shrines and images and breaks Moses' bronze serpent, which people had used for worship. He calls it Nehushtan. When Sennacherib attacks Judah's towns, Hezekiah pays the demand. He later prays after an Assyrian official's challenge. Kings describes the Lord's angel striking the Assyrian camp. In the illness account, Isaiah tells him to prepare for death. He prays and receives fifteen more years, with a backward-moving shadow as a sign. After he shows Babylonian envoys his treasures, Isaiah warns they will be carried to Babylon. These episodes do not establish an independent chronology here.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:2).

linked_stories.title: Hezekiah's Illness and the Babylonian Envoys

people.name: Manasseh
people.summary: Hezekiah's son, who becomes Judah's king at twelve and reigns fifty-five years. Kings describes him restoring shrines, building altars for Baal and heavenly bodies, and making his son pass through fire. It also describes his dealings with spirits and the innocent blood he sheds in Jerusalem. Kings reports a warning of disaster for Jerusalem because of his sins. Chronicles adds an account of Assyrian captains taking him in chains to Babylon. It says he humbles himself there and returns to Jerusalem. His son Amon follows him.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; rules from Jerusalem (2 Kings 21:1).

people.name: Josiah
people.summary: Amon and Jedidah's son, who becomes Judah's king at eight and reigns thirty-one years. Kings says he does right in the Lord's sight. In his eighteenth year, Hilkiah finds the law book in the temple. Josiah tears his clothes and sends to Huldah, a prophet. He reads the book to the people and makes an agreement to follow it. He removes idols and shrines in Judah and at Bethel. Kings links his actions at Bethel to an earlier prophet's words. It describes his Passover and his turning to the Lord as unequalled. Pharaoh-nechoh kills him at Megiddo.

linked_stories.title: The Man of God from Judah

people.name: Abner
people.summary: Ner's son and commander of Saul's army. First Samuel 14:50–51 supplies the family wording; this profile does not call Abner Saul's uncle. After Saul dies, Abner makes Ish-bosheth king at Mahanaim and leads his forces against David's men. During the fighting at Gibeon, he twice warns Asahel to stop pursuing him, then kills him with his spear. He quarrels with Ish-bosheth over Rizpah and offers to bring Israel over to David. David receives him at Hebron. Joab kills him at the gate; the account gives revenge for Asahel as the reason. David mourns publicly and walks behind his body.

people.name: Adonijah
people.summary: David's fourth son, born to Haggith after Absalom. As David ages, Adonijah declares he will be king, with chariots and fifty runners. Joab and Abiathar support him, and he holds a feast at En-rogel. Nathan and Bathsheba urge David to name Solomon. Adonijah flees to the altar and is spared on condition of good conduct. After David's death, he asks Bathsheba to request Abishag as his wife. Solomon sends Benaiah to kill him. This profile adds no hidden motive for Adonijah's request.

people.name: Amnon
people.summary: David's firstborn son, born at Hebron to Ahinoam. Second Samuel describes his desire for his half-sister Tamar and his distress. Following Jonadab's advice, he pretends to be ill and asks Tamar to bring food. He rapes her, then the account says his hatred exceeds his earlier desire. He has her thrown out. David is very angry, but this episode reports no action by him. Two years later, Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon during a sheep-shearing feast while Amnon is drinking wine.

residence: Baal-hazor, where he is killed (2 Samuel 13:23)

people.name: Tamar, daughter of David
people.summary: David's daughter and Absalom's sister, whom Second Samuel describes as beautiful. She wears the special garment of the king's unmarried daughters. David sends her to prepare food for Amnon. She begs Amnon not to force her and says he could ask the king for her. Amnon rapes her and throws her out. She tears her garment, puts ashes on her head and cries aloud. Absalom takes her in, and the account describes her remaining desolate in his house. She is distinct from Judah's daughter-in-law and from Absalom's daughter Tamar in 2 Samuel 14:27.

geography.origin: Jerusalem, in the king's house (2 Samuel 13:7)

people.name: Cyrus
people.summary: King of Persia, whose first-year proclamation in Ezra permits Judeans to return and rebuild Jerusalem's temple. He says the God of heaven gave him his kingdoms and calls God's people to go. He asks neighbours to help with silver, gold and goods. He returns temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar, counting them out to Sheshbazzar. Ezra links this to Jeremiah's words. Isaiah calls Cyrus the Lord's anointed, and Daniel says Daniel prospers into his reign. These texts do not say every Judean returned or establish Cyrus's birthplace.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; king of Persia in Ezra 1:1.

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Judah and Cyrus's Decree

people.name: Zerubbabel
people.summary: A leader among those returning from Babylon. Ezra and Haggai call him Shealtiel's son, while 1 Chronicles 3:19 lists him among Pedaiah's sons. This profile leaves that difference unresolved and does not identify him with Sheshbazzar. With Jeshua, he builds the altar and lays the temple foundation in the second year. After work stops, messages from Haggai and Zechariah prompt them to begin again. Haggai calls him Judah's governor and describes the Lord promising to make him a signet, a seal of authority. Zechariah says he will finish the temple. Matthew places him in Jechonias's family line.

geography.origin: Babylon, among the returnees led out in Cyrus's time (Ezra 2:2)

people.name: Ezra
people.summary: A priest from Aaron's line through Seraiah and a trained reader and teacher of Moses' law. In Artaxerxes' seventh year, he leaves Babylon with the king's letter on the first day of the first month. Ezra 7:9 places his arrival in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. The book says he prepares to study, follow and teach the law. After hearing about marriages to foreign women, he prays and weeps. Ezra 10:3 describes an agreement to send the women away. Nehemiah describes him reading the law to the people on the first day of the seventh month.

geography.origin: Priestly line of Aaron through Seraiah (Ezra 7:1-5)

people.name: Nehemiah
people.summary: Hachaliah's son, serving at Shushan when Hanani and others report Jerusalem's broken wall and the people's distress. He weeps, fasts and prays. In Artaxerxes' twentieth year, he serves the king's drink and asks to rebuild the city. He receives letters and timber. Nehemiah describes the wall builders facing opposition, carrying weapons as they work. He governs Judah for twelve years without taking the governor's food allowance. He later returns to the king, then comes back to make further reforms. This profile does not identify every Nehemiah in the records as this governor.

geography.origin: Shushan the palace, son of Hachaliah (Nehemiah 1:1)

people.name: Sanballat
people.summary: Called the Horonite in Nehemiah. With Tobiah and Geshem, he mocks the people rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. He speaks before Samaria's army. When the wall lacks only its doors, he sends four requests for Nehemiah to meet him near Ono. Nehemiah says they intend harm; this is Nehemiah's account of their purpose. Later, a son of Joiada from the high priest's family becomes Sanballat's son-in-law. Nehemiah drives that man away. The Horonite label is not used here to assign a modern nationality.

children: Daughter (unnamed), married into the high priest's family

residence: Samaria is named in his speech (Nehemiah 4:2)

people.name: Vashti
people.summary: Ahasuerus's queen, who holds a feast for women while he feasts with the princes. On the seventh day, the king is merry with wine. He sends seven court servants to bring her wearing the royal crown and display her beauty. She refuses, and he becomes angry. Esther gives no reason for her refusal. Memucan advises barring her from the king's presence and giving her position to another woman. A decree goes to every province. The later search for a queen leads to Esther taking her place.

geography.origin: Not stated in the text; queen of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:9)

people.name: Ahasuerus
people.summary: Esther's king ruling 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, with his throne at Shushan. In his third year, he displays his riches for 180 days, then gives a seven-day feast. He removes Vashti and makes Esther queen in his seventh year. He promotes Haman and gives his ring for the decree against the Jews. After Esther reveals the plot, he orders Haman's death and gives the ring to Mordecai. The book later says he imposes tribute on the land and islands. This profile does not settle his external historical identity.

geography.origin: King of Persia, 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia (Esther 1:1)

people.name: Esther
people.summary: Hadassah, Abihail's daughter, whose cousin Mordecai raises her as his own daughter after her parents die. Esther says she enters the king's house in the tenth month of his seventh year and becomes queen. At Mordecai's direction, she keeps her people secret. When Haman's decree comes, Mordecai says help may come elsewhere and her position may be for this moment. She asks the Jews to fast three days and approaches the king without being called. The book describes two banquets, her naming Haman and a second decree for the Jews.

geography.origin: Jewish orphan in Shushan, daughter of Abihail (Esther 2:7, 2:15)

people.name: Mordecai
people.summary: Jair's son from Benjamin, living in Shushan and raising his cousin Esther. Esther traces his family through Shimei and Kish. He tells Esther to conceal her people, uncovers Bigthan and Teresh's plot and refuses to bow to Haman. When Haman's decree comes, he tears his clothes, wears mourning cloth and urges Esther to act. The king honours him publicly using Haman's own proposal. He later receives the king's ring. Esther puts him in charge of Haman's house, which the king gave to her. He writes about keeping Purim and becomes second to the king. This profile distinguishes him from Ezra's returnee Mordecai.

people.name: Haman
people.summary: Hammedatha's son, called an Agagite, whom Ahasuerus promotes above the princes. When Mordecai refuses to bow, Haman seeks to destroy Mordecai's people. He casts a lot to choose the day and offers the king ten thousand talents of silver. Despite his invitations to Esther's banquets, seeing Mordecai angers him. On advice from Zeresh and friends, he builds a gallows fifty cubits high. The king makes him lead Mordecai through the city in honour. Esther names him as the enemy, and he is hanged on his own gallows. His house goes to Esther, and his ten sons are killed.

people.name: Daniel
people.summary: A child of Judah taken to Babylon and renamed Belteshazzar. Daniel says he refuses the king's food and wine and receives understanding of dreams and visions from God. He explains Nebuchadnezzar's dream and is made ruler over Babylon's province. He reads the writing for Belshazzar. Under Darius, he is thrown into a lions' den for praying despite a decree. Later chapters describe beasts, a ram and goat, seventy weeks and a final vision in Cyrus's third year. Ezekiel names a Daniel with Noah and Job; the shared name does not settle his identity here. Matthew records Jesus referring to Daniel as a prophet.

linked_stories.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar
people.summary: King of Babylon. Kings and Jeremiah describe his siege of Jerusalem, Jeconiah's captivity and the removal of temple vessels. His officers later burn the temple. Daniel describes his troubling dream of a statue and his promotion of Daniel over the wise men. He makes a gold image and orders three Judean men thrown into a furnace, then praises their God. Daniel also describes him living apart from people and eating grass like oxen. He later raises his eyes to heaven and praises its King. Cyrus returns the temple vessels he had taken. Daniel's father language about Belshazzar does not establish a biological link here.

linked_stories.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon
The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

people.name: Belshazzar
people.summary: Daniel calls him king of the Chaldeans. He feasts with a thousand lords and orders vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple brought out. The book describes a hand writing on the wall and his wise men failing to read it. The queen recalls Daniel. Daniel rebukes Belshazzar for not humbling himself despite knowing what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel reads and explains “Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin”. Belshazzar clothes him in scarlet but is killed that night. The book places other visions in Belshazzar's first and third years. Its father language for Nebuchadnezzar does not settle biological parentage here.

geography.origin: King of the Chaldeans; Nebuchadnezzar is called his father (Daniel 5:2, 5:22)

people.name: Jonah
people.summary: Amittai's son from Gathhepher, named as a prophet during Jeroboam son of Joash's reign. Jonah says the Lord sends him to Nineveh, but he flees toward Tarshish. Sailors throw him overboard during a storm. The book describes three days and nights in a great fish, where he prays. Sent again, he announces Nineveh's fall in forty days. The people believe God and fast. Jonah becomes angry and sits outside the city; the Lord asks whether Nineveh should be spared. The Gospels later describe Jesus speaking of Jonah's sign. This profile does not identify a fish species or make a science claim.

people.name: Isaiah
people.summary: Amoz's son, whose visions concern Judah and Jerusalem from Uzziah's reign to Hezekiah's. Isaiah describes seeing the Lord on a throne in the year Uzziah dies. He answers, “Here am I; send me”. He meets Ahaz with his son Shearjashub and offers the sign of Immanuel. Isaiah 8:3 describes a prophetess bearing his son without explicitly calling her his wife. Isaiah 20:3 describes his three years naked and barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia. He speaks to Hezekiah during the Assyrian crisis and his illness. He warns that Babylon will carry away Hezekiah's treasures and sons.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; his visions concern Judah and Jerusalem (Isaiah 1:1).

linked_stories.title: Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel

people.name: Ahaz
people.summary: Jotham's son, who becomes Judah's king at twenty and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem. Kings criticizes him for following Israel's kings, making his son pass through fire and offering sacrifices at shrines. When Syria and Israel threaten Jerusalem, Isaiah brings him a message to stay calm and not fear. Ahaz refuses the offered sign. Isaiah then gives the sign of Immanuel to David's family. This profile does not settle later readings of that sign. Hezekiah succeeds Ahaz.

linked_stories.title: Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel

people.name: Sennacherib
people.summary: King of Assyria, whom the biblical account places attacking Judah's fortified towns in Hezekiah's fourteenth year. Hezekiah offers tribute. Sennacherib sends Rabshakeh and other officials with a large army to Jerusalem's upper pool. Isaiah describes the Lord's angel striking the Assyrian camp, leaving 185,000 dead. The account says Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. Later, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer kill him in his god's temple, and Esarhaddon succeeds him.

geography.origin: Assyria; his capital in the text is Nineveh (Isaiah 37:37)

people.name: Jeremiah
people.summary: Hilkiah's son from the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin. His book describes receiving the Lord's words from Josiah's thirteenth year until Jerusalem's captivity. Told he was appointed a prophet before birth, he objects that he is young and cannot speak. Pashur strikes him and puts him in stocks. He opposes Hananiah's message and has Baruch write down his words. During Jerusalem's last siege, he is lowered into a pit and rescued by Ebed-melech. He later joins the group taken into Egypt against his warning.

geography.origin: Anathoth in the land of Benjamin (Jeremiah 1:1)

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

people.name: Baruch
people.summary: Neriah's son, who writes down Jeremiah's words. In Jehoiakim's fourth year, he records Jeremiah's spoken messages from the Lord on a scroll. After the king burns it, Baruch writes another at Jeremiah's direction, with further words added. The book says the Lord hides both men from arrest. A separate message to Baruch records his grief and lack of rest. After Jerusalem falls, he is taken into Egypt with Jeremiah. Shared family names do not expressly establish Seraiah as his brother.

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

people.name: Hananiah son of Azur
people.summary: Azur's son, a prophet from Gibeon, distinct from Daniel's companion. In Zedekiah's fourth year, he speaks before priests and people in the temple. He announces that the Lord has broken Babylon's power. He predicts the return of temple vessels, Jeconiah and the captives within two years. Jeremiah replies that the Lord did not send him and that his message makes people trust a lie. Jeremiah 28 says Hananiah dies that year, in the seventh month.

people.name: Zedekiah
people.summary: Josiah and Hamutal's son, named Mattaniah before the king of Babylon renames him Zedekiah in 2 Kings 24:17. He becomes Judah's king at twenty-one and reigns eleven years. The account criticizes his rule and describes his revolt against Babylon. During the siege, he secretly asks Jeremiah for the Lord's word. He lets the princes put Jeremiah in a pit, then allows Ebed-melech to lift him out. He asks Jeremiah to keep their talks secret. Babylonian forces catch him near Jericho, kill his sons before him, blind him and take him to Babylon. Jeremiah says he remains imprisoned until death.

parents: Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah

linked_stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt

people.name: Ebed-melech
people.summary: A court servant whom Jeremiah calls an Ethiopian eunuch, using an ancient designation associated with Cush. This label does not assign him a modern nationality. He hears Jeremiah has been put in a pit and appeals to the king at Benjamin's gate. With permission, he takes thirty men and lowers cloth and ropes to lift Jeremiah out. Jeremiah remains in the prison court. Jeremiah 39:18 presents the Lord's promise to save Ebed-melech when the city falls. The stated reason is his trust in the Lord.

geography.origin: Called Ethiopian in Jeremiah 38:7, an ancient designation associated with Cush; no modern nationality is assigned.

people.name: Ezekiel
people.summary: Buzi's son and a priest among captives by the river Chebar in Chaldea. His book places its opening visions in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity. It describes the heavens opening and visions of God. Addressed as “son of man”, Ezekiel is sent to speak and sits stunned among the exiles at Telabib. He is told to lie on his side as a sign of Israel's wrongdoing. The book describes his wife's death and a command not to mourn. Later, he describes the Spirit setting him in a valley of bones.

geography.origin: Priestly family, son of Buzi; among the exiles in Chaldea (Ezekiel 1:3)
residence: His house, with the elders of Judah (Ezekiel 8:1)

people.name: Hosea
people.summary: Beeri's son, whose book names four kings of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel. Hosea describes a command to marry a sexually unfaithful woman, followed by his marriage to Gomer. The children are named Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, with each name carrying a message to Israel. Chapter 3 tells him to love a woman involved with another man. He buys her for silver and barley and tells her to wait for him. The book links these actions to the Lord's love for Israel. Chapter 3 does not name the woman as Gomer.

people.name: Gomer
people.summary: Diblaim's daughter, whom Hosea marries following the Lord's command in Hosea 1. She bears a son, then a daughter named Lo-ruhamah. After weaning her, she bears another son, Lo-ammi. Chapter 3 describes an unnamed woman involved with another man. Hosea buys her and tells her to remain with him. The passage does not state that she is Gomer.

people.name: Amos
people.summary: A herdsman from Tekoa whose words concern Israel during Uzziah's and Jeroboam son of Joash's reigns. Amos 1 places them two years before an earthquake. Amaziah, Bethel's priest, reports him to the king and tells him to stop speaking there and return to Judah. In Amos 7:14–15, Amos says he was neither a prophet nor a prophet's son. He describes tending herds and gathering sycomore fruit. He says the Lord took him from his flock and sent him to Israel. This prophet is distinct from the Amos in Luke's family list.

people.name: Amaziah the priest of Bethel
people.summary: Bethel's priest, distinct from the king of Judah with the same name. In Amos 7, he tells Jeroboam that Amos is plotting against him and the land cannot bear his words. He reports a prediction of Jeroboam's violent death and Israel's captivity. Calling Amos “O thou seer”, he tells him to leave for Judah and earn his living by speaking there. He orders him to stop speaking at Bethel because it is the king's chapel and court.

people.name: Eliphaz
people.summary: Called the Temanite, he is one of Job's three friends. They agree to visit, mourn and comfort Job, and Eliphaz speaks first. At the close, the story describes the Lord rebuking him and the other two friends for their words about God. They are told to offer bulls and rams while Job prays for them. Genesis 36 names an Eliphaz in Esau's family; Job does not identify its speaker as that man.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

people.name: Bildad
people.summary: Called the Shuhite, he visits Job with Eliphaz and Zophar to mourn and comfort him. He speaks after Eliphaz. His arguments are his own speeches, not this profile's explanation of suffering. At the close, the story includes him in the Lord's rebuke of the three friends' words about God. He joins the others in making an offering while Job prays. The name Shuhite is retained without a further claim about his origin.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

people.name: Zophar
people.summary: Called the Naamathite, he agrees to visit Job with the other two friends and speaks in turn. His arguments remain his own speeches, not this profile's explanation of suffering. At the close, the story includes him in the Lord's rebuke. He joins the others in offering seven bulls and seven rams while Job prays. No further fate is supplied here.

residence: Came to Job in his affliction (Job 2:11)

people.name: Elihu
people.summary: Barachel's son, called a Buzite from Ram's family. Job 32 says he waits for the older speakers to finish. It describes his anger at Job for defending himself rather than God. He is also angry at the three friends for condemning Job without finding an answer. He speaks in chapters 32–37 and says he too is made of clay. The Lord's later rebuke does not name him. Job 2:11 describes the three friends' visit, not Elihu's journey or home.

residence: Not stated; he speaks to Job in Job 32:6.

people.name: Mary
people.summary: A virgin from Nazareth, engaged to Joseph of Nazareth. Luke describes Gabriel announcing that she will bear Jesus, and her reply, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”. She visits her relative Elisabeth and sings a prayer praising God. Luke places Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, where Mary lays him in a feeding trough. She presents him in the temple and later finds him there among the teachers. John places her at Cana's wedding and the cross, where Jesus entrusts her to the disciple he loved. Acts names her among those gathered after Jesus' ascent.

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
The Births of John and Jesus
Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Temple
The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

people.name: Joseph of Nazareth
people.summary: A man from David's family, engaged to Mary. Matthew calls him just and says he plans a private separation after learning she is pregnant. It describes an angel telling him to marry her and name the child Jesus. Luke places him with Mary at Bethlehem for registration. Matthew describes dream warnings leading him to take the family to Egypt and later return to Nazareth. Luke includes him at the temple presentation and the Passover visit when Jesus is twelve. These accounts describe his household relationship with Jesus without establishing biological parentage. These passages do not describe his later life. The Gospels do not name him at the cross.

children: Jesus (household relationship; no biological parentage inferred)

geography.origin: Nazareth in Galilee, of the house of David (Luke 1:27)

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth
The Births of John and Jesus
Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Temple

people.name: Elisabeth
people.summary: Zacharias's wife, whom Luke describes as righteous, childless and advanced in years. Luke calls her a daughter of Aaron, meaning a family line rather than an immediate father. After an announcement to Zacharias in the temple, she becomes pregnant and stays hidden for five months. When her relative Mary visits, Luke describes the child moving within her and Elisabeth being filled with the Holy Spirit. She blesses Mary as her Lord's mother. At her child's naming, she insists he be called John.

linked_stories.title: The Births of John and Jesus

people.name: Zacharias
people.summary: A priest from Abia's service group and Elisabeth's husband. Luke describes Gabriel telling him in the temple that Elisabeth will bear a son named John. Gabriel links Zacharias's loss of speech to his unbelief. On the eighth day, Zacharias writes, “His name is John”. His speech returns when the child is named, and he praises God. His speech describes a saving power raised in David's family. This profile does not settle the identity of the Zacharias in Matthew 23:35.

geography.origin: A priest of the course of Abia (Luke 1:5)

linked_stories.title: The Births of John and Jesus

people.name: John the Baptist
people.summary: Zacharias and Elisabeth's son. Luke places the announcement to Mary in Elisabeth's sixth month of pregnancy, without giving an exact interval between births. Matthew describes John preaching changed lives in Judaea's wilderness, wearing camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey. He baptizes people who confess their sins in the Jordan. Luke records advice to crowds, soldiers and tax collectors; Matthew describes his rebuke of Pharisees and Sadducees. He baptizes Jesus, and John records his statement that Jesus must increase while he decreases. After rebuking Herod over Herodias, he is imprisoned. He sends disciples to question Jesus before the account of his execution.

geography.origin: Hill country of Judaea, son of Zacharias and Elisabeth (Luke 1:39-40, 57-60)

linked_stories.title: The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus
John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
The Births of John and Jesus
The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana

people.name: Herod the king
people.summary: King of Judaea when Matthew places Jesus' birth. “Great” is a conventional label, not his quoted KJV name. Visiting wise men ask about the newborn king, troubling Herod and Jerusalem. Religious leaders name Bethlehem, and he tells the visitors to report back. Matthew says their return by another road angers him. He orders the killing of children aged two and under in Bethlehem and nearby areas. After his death, Matthew describes Joseph bringing the family from Egypt. Luke places John's birth in his reign. He is distinct from Herod the tetrarch and the Herod in Acts known as Agrippa.

linked_stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth

people.name: Peter
people.summary: A fisherman from Bethsaida, Andrew's brother, called Simon and named Peter by Jesus. Luke describes him leaving his nets after an extraordinary catch. The Gospels' calling accounts are kept distinct here. Peter comes first in lists of the Twelve. Matthew describes him walking on water, sinking and declaring, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”. Jesus rebukes him for resisting the warning of his coming suffering and death. Peter sees Jesus transformed on the mountain and later promises not to deny him. After the arrest, he denies Jesus three times and weeps. John describes his tomb visit and the risen Jesus asking about his love and directing him to feed his sheep.

linked_stories.title: Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.summary: One of the Twelve, named as Jesus' betrayer. John says he keeps the money bag and steals from it. His protest at the Bethany anointing lacks concern for the poor. Matthew describes his agreement with the priests for thirty silver pieces. At supper, he is identified as the betrayer. He later leads the arresting group and identifies Jesus with a kiss. Matthew says he repents, returns the silver and hangs himself. Acts gives a different death account; this profile does not combine them. The cited verses do not establish his birthplace.

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.summary: A woman called Magdalene, from whom Luke says seven devils had gone. She travels with Jesus and supports him from her resources. The Gospels place her among the women at the cross and describe her seeing his burial place. She finds the tomb's stone moved at dawn. John describes her weeping there and Jesus calling her by name. John says she tells the disciples that she has seen the Lord. The Gospels do not identify her with Luke 7's unnamed woman or Mary of Bethany. Her birthplace is not stated in the cited passage.

geography.origin: Birthplace not stated; Luke calls her Magdalene (Luke 8:2).

people.name: Martha
people.summary: Mary and Lazarus's sister from Bethany in John. Luke 10 describes a Martha welcoming Jesus and asking him to make Mary help with serving. Its village is unnamed, so the cross-account identity remains qualified here. In John, Martha meets Jesus after Lazarus dies and says, “if thou hadst been here”. She declares him the Christ and God's Son. At the tomb, she objects that the body will smell. John later describes her serving at a meal six days before Passover.

residence: Bethany (John 11:1); Luke 10:38 leaves its village unnamed.

linked_stories.title: The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha

people.name: Mary of Bethany
people.summary: Martha and Lazarus's sister from Bethany in John. Luke 10 describes a Mary hearing Jesus while Martha serves, but leaves the village unnamed. This profile keeps that cross-account identity qualified. In John, Mary remains home after Lazarus dies until she is called. She falls at Jesus' feet and says, “if thou hadst been here”. John describes Jesus weeping and raising Lazarus. Before Passover, Mary pours costly spikenard perfume on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects; Jesus links her act to his burial. Matthew and Mark leave their Bethany anointing woman unnamed. She is not identified here with Luke 7's unnamed woman.

linked_stories.title: The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha

people.name: Lazarus
people.summary: Martha and Mary's brother from Bethany, whom John says Jesus loves. He becomes ill and dies, spending four days in the grave before Jesus arrives. John describes Jesus thanking the Father and calling, “Lazarus, come forth”. Lazarus emerges in burial cloths, and Jesus tells others to free him. Many believe because of this account's event. Before Passover, Lazarus eats with Jesus, and the chief priests plan to kill him too. This Lazarus is distinct from the character in Luke 16's story.

people.name: Nicodemus
people.summary: A Pharisee, a member of a Jewish religious group, and a leader who visits Jesus at night in John. He says Jesus' miracles show God is with him. Jesus speaks of being born again through water and the Spirit: a new birth Nicodemus struggles to understand. The dialogue turns to the raised serpent and God's love in John 3:16. In John 7, Nicodemus asks whether the law judges someone before hearing him. After the crucifixion, he brings about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes, substances used in preparing a body. He helps Joseph of Arimathaea bury Jesus.

geography.origin: A Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews (John 3:1)

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.summary: The Roman governor of Judaea before whom Jesus appears after his arrest. The Gospels record him asking, “Art thou the King of the Jews?” and declaring no fault. Luke describes him sending Jesus to Herod. The accounts also describe the offer involving Barabbas; Matthew adds his wife's warning and his hand washing. He has Jesus whipped and hands him over for crucifixion. John gives the cross inscription as “Jesus Of Nazareth The King Of The Jews”. He grants Joseph of Arimathaea the body. Matthew describes a guard at the tomb. Luke 13:1 mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices.
